headline: Tk 34,497cr project: Padma Barrage construction to begin in early 2027
summary: The 2.1km long barrage will be built with government funds over seven years, aiming to boost agriculture and fisheries across 24 southwestern districts.
details: Water Resources Minister Shahiduddin Chowdhury Anee announced that construction of the Padma Barrage will begin next year, with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman expected to inaugurate the work between January and March 2027.
The BNP government has approved the project at a cost of Tk 34,497 crore. The 2.1-kilometre-long barrage will be implemented using government funds over the next seven years.
The project will feature 78 spillway gates, 18 undersluice gates, one navigation lock, and two fish passes. Additionally, a railway bridge will be constructed over the barrage.
Two hydroelectric power plants, each with a capacity of 113 megawatts, will also be built as part of the project. The technical survey for the barrage began back in 2004.
Minister Anee stated that the barrage will transform the economy of 24 southwestern districts by bringing major changes to the agriculture and fisheries sectors.
The project is expected to help control river erosion during the monsoon and resolve water shortages during the lean period, while also protecting the ecosystem of the Sundarbans.
caption:
A Tk 34,497 crore project to transform 24 southwestern districts is coming. Construction of the Padma Barrage begins in early 2027.

Water Resources Minister Shahiduddin Chowdhury Anee announced that construction of the Padma Barrage will begin next year, with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman expected to inaugurate the work between January and March 2027.

The BNP government has approved the project at a cost of Tk 34,497 crore. The 2.1-kilometre-long barrage will be implemented using government funds over the next seven years.

The project will feature 78 spillway gates, 18 undersluice gates, one navigation lock, and two fish passes. Additionally, a railway bridge will be constructed over the barrage.

Two hydroelectric power plants, each with a capacity of 113 megawatts, will also be built as part of the project. The technical survey for the barrage began back in 2004.

Minister Anee stated that the barrage will transform the economy of 24 southwestern districts by bringing major changes to the agriculture and fisheries sectors.

The project is expected to help control river erosion during the monsoon and resolve water shortages during the lean period, while also protecting the ecosystem of the Sundarbans.

headline_marked: TIB warns [[draft cyber law could enable unchecked surveillance]] and repression
headline: TIB warns draft cyber law could enable unchecked surveillance and repression
summary: Transparency International Bangladesh says the proposed Cyber Security (Amendment) Act 2026 poses serious risks to fundamental human rights and freedom of speech.
details: Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB) has warned that the draft Cyber Security (Amendment) Act 2026 could turn the country's cyberspace into an environment of unchecked surveillance and repression.

TIB Executive Director Dr Iftekharuzzaman stated that the draft conflates cybercrime, cybersecurity, and freedom of expression under one law, creating scope for deliberate misinterpretation and misuse.
The organization highlighted that vague definitions of terms like 'rumour', 'misinformation', and 'insulting to the state' could be used to target freedom of speech and fundamental rights.
Concerns were also raised over Section 46(2), which makes certain offences non-bailable and introduces ambiguous concepts regarding 'friendly relations with a foreign state'.
TIB criticized the proposed National Cyber Security Council, noting it would be dominated by government authority with very few independent experts.

The watchdog also questioned a provision that grants immunity to council members and officials for actions taken in 'good faith', calling it inconsistent with the principle of equality before the law.
TIB has called for a comprehensive revision of the draft law in line with international best practices and stakeholder views, reminding the ruling BNP of its manifesto commitments.
caption:
Could Bangladesh's cyberspace become a tool for repression? TIB warns a new draft cyber law poses serious risks to free speech.

Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB) has warned that the draft Cyber Security (Amendment) Act 2026 could turn the country's cyberspace into an environment of unchecked surveillance and repression.

TIB Executive Director Dr Iftekharuzzaman stated that the draft conflates cybercrime, cybersecurity, and freedom of expression under one law, creating scope for deliberate misinterpretation and misuse.

The organization highlighted that vague definitions of terms like 'rumour', 'misinformation', and 'insulting to the state' could be used to target freedom of speech and fundamental rights.

Concerns were also raised over Section 46(2), which makes certain offences non-bailable and introduces ambiguous concepts regarding 'friendly relations with a foreign state'.

TIB criticized the proposed National Cyber Security Council, noting it would be dominated by government authority with very few independent experts.

The watchdog also questioned a provision that grants immunity to council members and officials for actions taken in 'good faith', calling it inconsistent with the principle of equality before the law.

TIB has called for a comprehensive revision of the draft law in line with international best practices and stakeholder views, reminding the ruling BNP of its manifesto commitments.
